title: The Lord's Prayer: Structure, Petitions, and Proper Use
speaker: Mr. Nick Newton
summary: This lesson examines Westminster Larger Catechism questions 187 and 188 regarding the Lord's Prayer, analyzing its three-part structure (preface, petitions, and conclusion) and six petitions while emphasizing that God's glory should be the foremost goal of prayer. The instruction covers proper use of the Lord's Prayer as both a pattern and a prayer itself, warning against vain repetition and mechanical, liturgical misuse, and providing practical applications for personal prayer, ministry to new believers, and teaching children.

outline.title: Context and Foundational Principles
subpoints: Prayer as a conversation and relationship with God
God's glory as the foremost goal of the Lord's Prayer
The revealed will of God for prayer in Matthew and Luke
Proper worship limited by God's revealed will in Scripture

outline.title: The Three-Part Structure of the Lord's Prayer (Question 188)
subpoints: The preface: addressing God with reverence and holiness
The petitions: six sincere supplications to the sovereign God
The conclusion: affirming God's kingdom, power, and glory

outline.title: The Six Petitions Explained
subpoints: First petition: Hallowed be Thy name - regarding all God's revelation as holy
Second and third petitions: Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done - Christ's return and church growth
Fourth petition: Give us this day our daily bread - dependence on God's provision and contentment
Fifth petition: Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors - forgiveness proportionate to grace received
Sixth petition: Deliver us from temptation and evil - asking for God's protection and sanctification

outline.title: The Conclusion and God's Attributes
subpoints: Kingdom, power, and glory affirm God's sovereignty and excellency
Comfort in God's supreme control over all creation
Contrast with false religions that promote fear rather than mercy
Assurance of living under a merciful and gracious heavenly king

outline.title: Proper Use of the Lord's Prayer (Question 187)
subpoints: Two functions: as a pattern for prayer and as a prayer itself
Requirements: understanding, faith, reverence, and other necessary graces
Understanding must be genuine, not rote recitation
Faith that God hears and answers prayers
The importance of desire and focus in prayer

outline.title: Warnings Against Improper Use
subpoints: Avoiding vain repetitions and mechanical, liturgical use
Not seeking personal glory through prayer
Rejecting traditions that trivialize Christ's words
Example of Catholic penance practice devaluing the model prayer
The danger of straying from Christ's direct instruction

outline.title: Practical Applications for Daily Life
subpoints: Personal prayer: let the petitions shape your own prayers
Ministry to new believers: use the model prayer to jumpstart prayer life
Teaching children: progressively deepen understanding with age

transcript:
## Opening

It is a pleasure to have been asked to teach in front of you this morning. Let's open our Bibles to Matthew chapter 6. We're going to be studying the Lord's Prayer today.

## Scripture Reading

> So, take heed that you do not do your charitable deeds before men to be seen by them. Otherwise, you have no reward from your Father in heaven. Therefore, when you do a charitable deed, do not sound a trumpet before you as the hypocrites do in the synagogue and in the streets. They may have glory from men. Assuredly, I say to you, they have their reward. But when you do a charitable deed, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. Your charitable deed may be done in secret and your Father who sees in secret will himself reward you openly. And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets that they may be seen by men. Assuredly, I say to you, they have their reward. But you, when you pray, go into your room and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in the secret place and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. And when you pray, do not use vain repetitions as to heathen do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Therefore, do not be like them, for your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him. In this manner, therefore pray, our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread and forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen. (Matthew 6:1-13)

## Introduction and Overview

I've been blessed with the opportunity to speak on Westminster Larger Catechism questions 187 and 188 this morning. Those being, how is the Lord's Prayer to be used and of how many parts does the Lord's Prayer consist? We're going to work backwards though. We're going to start with question 188. We'll look at the text of the Lord's Prayer and try to more deeply understand exactly what we're called to pray for in the petitions. And then we'll circle back to 187 and look at the importance of truly knowing and understanding what we're praying and how we can apply the model prayer to our lives.

I owe a lot of this lesson to J.G. Voss's commentary on the catechism as well as Sinclair Ferguson's work on the Lord's Prayer. So if you hear something that really sticks, thank them.

In his book, "Habits of Grace," David Matthews describes prayer as a conversation we did not start, but a relationship into which we are drawn. It is our duty to behold this relationship with the Almighty God in reverence and understanding, as we'll see in question 187. I'll be using the titles "Lord's Prayer" and "Model Prayer" interchangeably today.

Last week, Alex shared question 185 with us, asking us, how are we to pray? That is, what sort of affections are we to espouse as we pray? We're called to pray with a deep sense of our own unworthiness, penitent and thankful hearts, humble submission to his will, and an awful apprehension of the majesty of God, which I believe is arguably the most important there.

This morning, we're going to look at the instructions for acceptable prayer to God the Father, given us directly by his Son. My aim is to show that God's glory is the foremost goal of the Lord's Prayer, and it should be our goal in our personal prayer as well. Through the structure and wording of Christ's Model Prayer and how the confession calls us to use the Lord's Prayer in our spiritual lives.

## Foundational Principles on Prayer and Worship

The Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 21, paragraph 1, reads in part:

> The acceptable way of worshiping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will that he may not be worshiped any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture.

This passage opens the chapter on proper worship, but it can be applied to prayer as well without much of a stretch. In the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, God reveals his will for how we are to pray in his Son's institution of the Lord's Prayer. As a result, we're provided with not only a pattern of words to consider, but a template for our thoughts to keep God's glory at the forefront of our prayers.

So, start with this question. What are some overarching themes we can find in the Lord's Prayer? Thankfulness. Deliverance. Obedience. Forgiveness. Debt. All right, these are all very good answers. There are many more good answers as well. But what Christ seems to focus on is that God's own glory and not our supplications is to be front and center within prayer.

Consider the words of Psalm 150:

> Praise the Lord. Praise God in his sanctuary. Praise him in his mighty firmament. Praise him for his mighty acts. Praise him according to his excellent greatness.

In Matthew 6, we see Jesus extolling the excellent greatness of the Heavenly Father. He opens with a declaration of God's glorified place in heaven, verse 9. Every petition seeks an increase of God's glory, whether directly resulting from what is prayed for, verses 10 through 13. And finally, the conclusion ascribes once more his supremacy, the honor he is due at the end of the verse, verse 13. Thus, we should hold to that standard in our own prayer lives. Let's have that mindset that looks for ways to tie every aspect of prayer back to glorifying God as we look at the specific petitions.

## Question 188: The Three Parts of the Lord's Prayer

So question 188 asks a simple question of how many parts the Lord's Prayer consists. The answer is equally simple. The Lord's Prayer consists of three parts: a preface, petitions, and a conclusion. I'd like to think this was the last question they had to knock out before they broke for lunch. Seriously though, each division of the prayer deserves legitimate consideration.

In normal conversation, you don't just go up to someone and immediately begin rambling until you run out of things to spout and then walk off. Nevertheless, we're taught to approach prayer in an organized way. We ought to have something of a plan before we entreat the God of heaven and earth. Our God is worthy of all glory and honor and power in Revelation 4:11. How much more worthy is He of His people making a little effort in their prayers?

In his commentary on question 188, J.G. Voss implores that we should not rush into God's holy presence and begin to talk about our personal needs without first addressing Him in a reverent and worthy manner. So not only must we pray with structure, we're called to draw up each part, start to finish in a way that makes everything of His glory and nothing of us.

When we keep that at the front of our minds, God's holiness and our fallenness, God's infinity and our finitude, the dynamic of our prayer should be forced away from casualness. And with that, I'll cap off my thoughts on the preface.

## The Petitions

### Introduction to Petitions

The largest division of the Lord's Prayer is the petitions. These aren't the kind of petitions that come to mind when someone mentions change.org. That sort of petition is the polar opposite of prayer, using inflammatory language intended to wrench your heartstrings into agreement with the cause. Petitions in prayer are sincere, solemn supplications to the sovereign God, understanding our weakness and His might. The Lord's Prayer contains six of them. One will quickly notice how broad the categories are.

### First Petition: Hallowed Be Thy Name

The first petition is, "Hallowed be Thy Name." At first glance, we might see this as Christ relating a desire for the first three commandments to be upheld in Exodus 20, verses 3 through 7, and that is completely valid. If you had asked me how to describe the Lord's Prayer two weeks ago, I probably would have called it good with that explanation and moved on. There's much more depth to it, though.

Vos defines the word "hallowed" as to regard and treat as holy. Now, we know that when we discuss God's holiness, His name is not the limit of it. The six-winged creatures of Revelation 4:8 cry out:

> Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and is, and is to come.

So not only is the name of the Lord to be regarded as holy, but His entire eternal existence and all that has been revealed of it. Vos writes that this petition covers not merely names, but all which God makes himself known, His titles, attributes, ordinances, word, works, etc. All these constitute God's revelation of Himself, therefore, there to be regarded and treated as holy.

When we pray this first petition, we pray alongside Paul in 2 Thessalonians 3 that the word of the Lord may run swiftly and be glorified, and in its doing so, no dishonor will graze it at our hands or others.

### Second and Third Petitions: Thy Kingdom Come, Thy Will Be Done

The second and third petitions, "Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done," go hand in hand. Our prayer should be that the day of Christ's return will arrive sooner than later. Likewise, our prayer should ask that His church would increase in the interim. We are pleading the cause of the gospel itself as it is written in Matthew 24:14:

> This gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a witness to all the nations, and in the end will come.

But we also lift up the kingdom as we behold it today, the growth and sustainment of the visible body of believers, desiring growth in numbers, by salvation, and in spirit, by sanctification. We ask for growth and understanding through faithful proclamation of the gospel and to become stronger ministers of it. We ask for favor from the authorities, 1 Timothy 2:1-3. We ask that the light of life in Christ would increase and the darkness of the world decrease. Praying with Paul that the mystery of the gospel will be boldly proclaimed in Ephesians 6:19.

We ask all this not just for O.B.P.C. or for the Presbyterian denomination, but as the text says, every church that faithfully proclaims the name of Christ. These are your brethren in Christ. These are who we must have in mind as we pray, awaiting when all things are made new by Him who sits on the throne, Revelation 21:5.

Now we come to the third petition when we pray that God's will be done. At first glance, it's almost a silly way to word it. Of course, the only will that will ultimately be followed by the whole universe is God's will. God's will is sovereign. Positively, nothing comes to pass that was not ordained down to the moment by our Almighty God. Why would we measly humans be asking that God do what He's already set forth in eternity?

What Christ teaches us to communicate in simple language here is our acknowledgement and perhaps joy that we are not the be all end all. We are not the captain of our ship. We're caught in the crossfire of wills between God and Satan, and God's grace strengthens us and protects us. By the power of the Holy Spirit, we make the conscious effort to go against our sin nature. We happily submit to a plan of providence beyond our understanding.

In that same breath, we ask for the grace necessary to live for His glory as His revealed will commands. When God's glory is followed, His glory is increased.

Sinclair Ferguson puts it very well. When we pray, "Thy will be done," we are submitting to the Lord's Decretive Will. That is His sovereign purposes. But we're also asking for the help we need to understand and pursue His revealed will. The pattern of life He's set before us in Scripture, together with its rich and varied and many individual applications to our own lives.

### Fourth Petition: Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread

In the fourth petition, we're instructed to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread." Christ evokes the 16th chapter of Exodus here, where God provided exactly enough manna and quail to sustain His people for each passing day.

We have a daily dependence on God's providence to supply the needs that we have that are basic and fundamental to our lives. In other words, we don't exist without God allowing us to exist. In the model prayer, we're to ask God for the sustenance to make it through each day. And by implication, we acknowledge our frailty as fallen humans, requiring the gracious gift of God just to make it to the next sunrise.

The word "our" is also of some importance. The plural nature tells us that we're to pray for our brethren's provision as well. You may have friends who are struggling to make ends meet each week. Even if you aren't in a position to help physically, don't neglect them in your prayers. Oftentimes, offering prayer is the only thing we can do for someone, regardless of what ails them. All the more, we should pray for the provision of health and life itself for our family in Christ.

It's easy to get wrapped up in our personal or familial needs each day. I'm guilty of that. But Paul calls us to make supplication for all men in 1 Timothy 2.

On another note, we're praying for more than just food. When God supplies the means to provide, we ought to use them. If you're searching for work day to day and you're offered a job one morning, that is your daily bread.

In his work, "A Simple Way to Pray," Martin Luther brings another interesting idea under the umbrella of this petition:

> I commend to thee my house and property, wife and child. Grant that I may manage them well, supporting and educating them as a Christian should.

In essence, he is asking for the provision of a godly leader for his family and estate, and asking for the wherewithal for him to meet the challenge. That's a more layered take on the idea of provision than I would have come up with.

Anyways, this petition itself may be one of the easiest to wrap our heads around. But the flip side, though, is a little bit uncomfortable. In praying for enough to sustain us day by day, we must then be content with however much or little God sees fit to provide. If you pray for your daily bread and also a GMC Denali heavy duty Duramax, you will come out with everything you need for the day and likely more as our God is gracious, but you probably won't have a new pickup truck. Is that a problem for us? If we tend to hold against God the earthly things that we desire and don't have, maybe we got to look at our hearts. The whole point of praying for provision, day by day, is to refocus on our hearts, on how insignificant our human lives are and how greatly we need God's generosity.

We can take a look at Paul if we need a role model on contentment. The man was shipwrecked three times and yet God sustained him to make it through each day until he was called home, 2 Corinthians 11:25. In his own words:

> I have learned in whatever state I am to be content. I know how to be abased. I know how to abound. Everywhere and in all things, I have learned both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. (Philippians 4:11-12)

Earthly means were of little value to Paul. He took the blessings with thanksgiving, the hard times in stride and continued to serve his Lord throughout. In short, the lesson here is this. We must pray for contentment alongside provision. When we do, our hearts will be joyful to receive both abundant blessings or just enough to hack it. Either way, God brought you to the next day, which is a new opportunity to trust and glorify him more.

### Fifth Petition: Forgive Us Our Debts as We Forgive Our Debtors

In the fifth petition, we ask that God would forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. Now, the crucial word here is "as."

Christ himself gave us a whole parable detailing the dangers of not forgiving as we have been forgiven in Matthew 18. Later, Paul builds on this idea, calling the Ephesians:

> Do not let the sun go down on your anger (Ephesians 4:26)

God has forgiven the insurmountable debt of sinning before his holiness. Thus, we truly have no excuse not to forgive someone who has grieved us in this earthly life. Unfortunately, it's rarely that easy. We're wrong to greater degrees at different points in our life. As sinfully disposed humans, grudges come naturally. I'll raise my hand here. I often let grudges build without even consciously realizing it. Simply by changing my attitude towards the person.

But R.C. Sproul addresses this petition specifically. Here is where the conjunction "as" comes in. He relates the concept driving this petition as a real wake-up call. "Lord, please be as gracious to me as I am to those who have offended and violated me." Or, "Dear God, please give the same proportionate amount of mercy to me as I give to my enemies." That kicks things up a notch, huh?

It appeals to our own desires for favor with God while spurring us to tenderheartedness with others. That said, this petition, like all others, should encourage us to happily act on it. We should find comfort knowing that God is merciful to forgive when we ask because of the shed blood of his Son. Such treatment from our Heavenly Father, plus the calling to live more like our Savior, ought to equal no option other than willingness to forgive in our hearts.

### Sixth Petition: Deliver Us from Temptation and Evil

In this sixth petition, we are directed to pray, "Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one."

The Greek word here, "pyrausmos," can translate test, trial, and temptation. So we're not only asking for reprieve from sinful solicitations, but from the struggles God walks us through for our own strengthening. For some, the wording of the first half can be a sticking point. It is easily explained, though, by God's providence. What Satan means for evil, God will use as means for good. Christ shows us that there is a balance to be found in this. We are called to grin and bear our trials and temptations. But on the flip side, it's okay to ask for a break. As fallen humans, we will always be susceptible to Satan's enticements. And at times, God will grant our request, and the temptation, or thorn in the flesh, will leave us for a time. Other times, we must take 1 Corinthians 10:13 to heart:

> No temptation has overtaken you, except such as is common to man. But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape that you might be able to bear it.

Christ himself was tempted, just as we are in Matthew 4. Without that happening, the very covenant of works would not have been complete. All that to say, our Heavenly Father will never draw us into temptation himself, but he will use these situations within his will to sanctify us. So we ought to pray for God to buffet Satan's attacks, as sin and its temptations are not glorifying to himself. We also ought to acknowledge our state of vulnerability to sin and our desire to grow closer to God. Either way, we petition for an increase of God and a decrease of evil that we may see more of His glory in our spiritual lives.

## The Conclusion

And finally, we come to the conclusion of the prayer: "For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory forever. Amen."

The conclusion echoes the theme of God's glory, bringing that emphasis full circle. There is a thoughtful succinctness to it. These three words—kingdom, power, and glory—summarize great theological truths. This conclusion should remind us of the blessing we have to be under the rule of a merciful heavenly king, as pilgrims on earth and citizens of heaven. We affirm his sovereignty, omnipotence, and glorious excellency, as the Catechism later says, over all creation, from eternity past through eternity future.

These words should comfort us that the God of the Bible is the one true God, the only one in supreme control. If our God was anything other than the fullness of His revealed attributes, life on earth would be much worse. For example, those deceived by false religions like Islam live their lives in fear of a sovereign yet unmerciful God. As followers of Christ, though, we're received into the kingdom that cannot be shaken by mercy and grace, not of any merit within us. Ephesians 2:8-9 and Hebrews 12:28. The Catechism begs us to see that this is who we lift our prayers to. In doing so, it calls us to keep God's attributes in view for the duration of every prayer we make.

Beloved, if nothing else strikes you today, let it be this. God is our sovereign, merciful king. He's worthy of your eternal glory. Find your comfort in this.

## Question 187: How to Use the Lord's Prayer

Now we come to question 187. So now we come to question 187: How is the Lord's Prayer to be used?

The Catechism answers: "The Lord's Prayer is not only for direction as a pattern according to which we make our prayers, but may also be used as a prayer so that it be done with understanding, faith, reverence, and other graces necessary to the right performance and duty of prayer."

Before we jump in, I'll add this little preface. Question 187 is essentially a comprehensive application of the Lord's Prayer. At prayer, you'll find some bits and pieces from this section useful as such. We find the two functions described here in the differences of wording used between Matthew and Luke. Matthew 6:9 reads, "In this manner, therefore, pray," while Luke 11:2 reads, "When you pray."

In our Wednesday night sermons, the pastor has stressed that different gospel authors record the same event in different verbiage to emphasize different aspects for different purposes. The Holy Spirit inspired these differences so they're not to be ignored. The Catechism teaches that that's what we're looking at here, citing Matthew 6:9 for use as a template and Luke 11:2 for its standalone use.

### Understanding in Prayer

The answer then says we're to use it with understanding, faith, reverence, and other graces necessary to the duty of prayer. In other words, at no point are Christ's words of instruction to be treated as a tool of liturgy merely.

As far as understanding goes, we may ask this question: What is the depth of our reasoning for praying the Lord's Prayer? We're supposed to pray scripture—valid. But are you truly seeking to gain from it? If you can recite it in your sleep, good for you, but what have you ultimately profited? That's a fair question.

### Faith in Prayer

In addition, we must have true faith that God will hear and answer our petitions, trusting the words of 1 Peter 3:12:

> For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are open to their prayers.

That's not just wishful thinking, that is the truth. We also ought not to approach this prayer in a lackadaisical way, as if we tire of hearing or saying it. That breeds irreverence, and we'll tire God with it. As often as we hear these words, we should consider them for what they are. The words of God the Son, addressed to God the Father, recorded through God the Spirit to bless us.

### Other Necessary Graces

We've come to the last piece of this answer: "other graces necessary to the right performance and duty of prayer."

Words are hard. Anyone listening who's recently sought employment knows what the divines did here. Job postings detail what will be expected of the worker, but they always have that one clause at the bottom: "and other duties as assigned." It's a catch-all with the expectation of adapting to whatever the job throws at you. The assembly had the same idea here. Each of us may have different struggles in our prayers. Understanding, faith, and reverence cover a lot of that—mindless praying, prayer without trusting its effectiveness, praying with a cluttered mind. But what could some of the other graces necessary to prayer be? I would encourage all of you to study that on your own, see what you all come up with. But I will propose one more briefly.

We ought to pray with a desire to pray. We should truly want to devote our time and mental faculties to our conversations with God. We see this in Christ's example in Mark 1:35:

> Now in the morning, having risen a long while before daylight, he went out and departed to a solitary place. And there he prayed.

Christ gives us this example as a command to overcome what's definitely my largest struggle with prayer: making time, even if it's uncomfortable. A lot of us are no strangers to waking up before daylight. For me, waking up even earlier than I have to is not what I would prefer to do. But I know it's likely the only time of day where I'll be able to fully focus on prayer. My next biggest struggle is desiring to pray enough to clear my mind. Escaping the mental planning for the day is a challenge for me. But Christ did what he had to for clarity. He went to a solitary place away from the clamor of civilization in general, so he would be physically and mentally undisturbed. In other words, he wasn't getting notifications and buzzes. His microwave wasn't beeping. You get the picture. In similar fashion, we ought to find a place where we're able to devote that same focus. A conversation with our Heavenly Father will always be worth it.

## Warnings Against Improper Use

I believe it would be wrong not to touch on the improper uses of the model prayer that can be pointed out even today. Alex gave us a good primer on it last week. In Matthew 6:5-8, before he lays out his prayer, Christ himself warns us against treating prayers anything other than coming before the eternal throne. We are to seek positively no personal glory through our prayer and avoid trivializing the words of Christ so that we might remain focused on a prayer which glorifies God.

Some parties object to the verbatim use of the Lord's Prayer in its original form, citing verse 7 that condemns secular religions for vain repetitions, "for they think that they will be heard by their many words." But if we follow the guidance of the Catechism, vain repetitions are exactly what our prayers are not. That is why we spend so much time digging into the prayer itself.

However, we should briefly note the result of misunderstanding the model prayer, treating it as a mechanical, liturgical device. The Westminster Divines observed this in the traditions they sought to reform. So we have question 187. J.G. Voss echoes the scripture and Catechism, writing that those who use the Lord's Prayer as a formality or a repetitive chant:

> Do not have the slightest understanding of its true nature and proper use.

Not pulling any punches there. A common example is the Roman Catholic practice of repetitive prayer for penance on orders of the priest. I've found that most Catholic sources try to downplay this tradition, so you'd think that there's at least some internal acknowledgement of that systemic issue there. If you need a real life example, though, you can ask my grandma how many Our Fathers she had to say after fighting with her brother and sister as a kid. That's not a joke. That is the reality of how they use the Lord's Prayer. In short, Roman Catholic tradition devalues the words Christ himself gave us to mold how we approach our holy God. This proves how easy it can be to miss the point of the model prayer, and as a result, prayer in general.

Christ did not give his disciples any liberty to choose whom they prayed to. The Holy Spirit gave us one model to follow with one direct object to address our prayers unto: our Heavenly Father. We are not to tarnish the glory due God by polluting prayer with human add-ons and traditions. Not understanding the gravity of Christ's instruction puts us merely steps away from an unacceptable disservice to our Savior and Heavenly Father.

As we well know, all scripture is useful for training in righteousness, 2 Timothy 3:16-17. The premise of the model prayer is instruction to follow. Christ intended it to be straightforward and succinct. Therefore, it's an ideal tool for those who want or need to grow in the discipline of prayer.

## Practical Applications for Daily Life

As we wrap up, let's see a few ways we can actively use the understanding of the Lord's Prayer in daily life.

### Personal Prayers

Let the knowledge of these petitions, what they signify and communicate, shape your prayer. We should contemplate them outside of prayer time to shape our own petitions inspired by the depth of the subjects Christ covers. We should harness our understanding of this model to relate our own needs through the framework Christ gave us.

### Ministry to New Believers

If you're ministering to someone who has little to no experience praying, it may seem daunting to them. I bet we've all seen examples of this. The model prayer is a perfect way to jumpstart their prayer life. They don't have to figure out what to say. That's often a sticking point for people. From that point, the door is open to study the petitions with them, like we did today, as deeply as you both can handle. The Lord's Prayer provides a great means to share and study the gospel in a way that directly relates to our lives.

### Teaching Children

Similarly, we could use the same method on a different scale to instruct children in how to pray. Deeper and deeper study could follow with age. Kids may benefit later in life if they have practiced meaningful conversations with their Savior.
